## FAQ

### Which editors does suggesting mode support?

Anything that renders on the web. Suggestion targets are DOM elements, so inputs, selects, table cells, contenteditable surfaces, and your own custom components work through the same attribute and anchor API; editor libraries connect through their setups.

### How do I add suggesting mode to a React app?

Install @veltdev/react, set up Velt Comments (the accept and reject buttons render on the comment dialog), tag elements with data-velt-suggestion-target, and call enableSuggestionMode. Handle the suggestionAccepted event to apply accepted values to your state or backend.

### Can AI agents propose changes through suggestions?

Yes. An agent's proposed value is committed as a pending suggestion on the exact target, and a human accepts or rejects it before anything is applied. The agent never holds write access to your data.

### What happens when a suggestion is accepted?

Velt records the outcome and fires suggestionAccepted with the old and new values; your handler applies the change to your state or backend. The SDK never mutates your data. Rejections fire suggestionRejected with an optional reason, and nothing is applied.

### What if the content changed before a reviewer accepts?

If the target no longer resolves at accept time, the suggestion goes stale instead of applying. If the live value moved since the proposal was captured, a drift flag is recorded (best-effort, requires a registered getter); in v1, the accept still applies, with a confirmation prompt planned. A stale target never applies.

### Do suggestions require Velt Comments?

Yes. A suggestion is stored as a comment annotation of type suggestion, and the accept and reject UI renders on the comment dialog, so Comments must be set up first. See /comments.

### Can I build my own suggestion UI?

Yes. Restyle the comment dialog with wireframes and primitives, and query suggestions by target or status to drive your own badges, counts, and review panels.

### What does it cost to add suggesting mode?

Velt is priced on usage, not seats: you pay for documents with review activity in a month, and there is a free tier for development and early production. Suggestions is part of the SDK, not a separately priced add-on.

# Webhooks & API
https://velt.dev/webhooks-and-api

Integrate seamlessly with your systems for extended functionality


## FAQ

### What can I do with the REST API?

Programmatically perform CRUD operations on every Velt feature — comments, organizations, users, documents, recordings, notifications. The same data your frontend sees is available server-side via signed REST endpoints.

### How are webhooks signed?

Each webhook payload is signed with HMAC SHA-256 using your project's secret. Verify the X-Velt-Signature header before processing. Failed signature checks are dropped and retried.

### What are the rate limits?

Default 100 requests per second per API key, with burst capacity for write traffic. Reach out for higher limits — enterprise plans get custom quotas plus dedicated retry queues.

Every quarter spent on this is a quarter not spent on your own product.

**Do they interop with Apryse annotations?** Yes. The Velt adapter maps to Apryse's annotation layer so native and Velt annotations coexist on the same document.

**Can an agent flag a region, for counsel to approve?** Yes. An agent posts a comment or suggestion on the region as a first-class user, and a human approves or rejects before anything changes.

**Is there an exportable record for the security review?** Yes. The audit trail captures every markup and approval on the matter and is exportable via API.

**How is Velt priced?** On usage, not seats or integrations: you pay for documents with review activity in a month, with a free tier for development and early production.

- Reactions trigger bot actions (reading works on all plans; writing reactions needs a self-hosted reactions service).
- One bot, many platforms on one Chat SDK codebase.

## Setup

@veltdev/chat-sdk-adapter plus a webhook endpoint; docs velt.dev/docs/ai/chat-sdk-adapter.

## FAQ

**How is a bot triggered?** A Velt webhook fires on @-mention or reaction: comment.add, comment_annotation.add, comment.reaction_add, or comment.reaction_delete.

**Can the same bot run on Slack and Velt?** Yes. The Chat SDK adapter maps Velt threads to the Chat SDK's channel and message model, so the same bot codebase runs on Velt, Slack, Discord, and every other Chat SDK adapter.

**How is Velt priced?** On usage, not seats or integrations: you pay for documents with review activity in a month, with a free tier for development and early production.

# Comments and co-editing, built for Lexical
https://velt.dev/libraries/lexical

Add comments and co-editing, plus live presence, to your Lexical editor, for your users and your AI agents. Threads stay pinned to nodes as the document tree updates, and every agent edit lands as a suggestion your users approve, so a comment on a heading never jumps to the paragraph below it.

## Build this into Lexical yourself, and you rebuild it on every release.

Your users expect to comment and co-edit in Lexical, and your AI agents need that same editor with a human approving before they touch user work. Comments that survive Lexical's node-tree updates are a multi-quarter build, and the moment anchoring breaks, feedback lands on the wrong node. Co-editing is the harder half: rolled by hand it means overwrites, lost work, and merge conflicts, the "my changes disappeared" bug reports, plus a websocket fleet and offline merge to keep alive. And the harder question is your agents: a useful agent needs to change the work, but an agent with write access to user content is what your buyers' security review blocks, so without a consent step you choose between an agent that is useful and an agent that is safe. Every quarter spent on this is a quarter not spent on your own product.

## Built for Lexical

Velt is the review and collaboration layer built for Lexical: your users and your AI agents work the same editor, with comment threads anchored to the node, and every agent suggestion is a change a human approves before it lands.

## Features

- **Agents as first-class users**: Your AI agent comments and suggests on the editor as a first-class user; a human approves or rejects, and on approve the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record. (https://velt.dev/review-agents)
- **Comments**: Threaded comments on nodes and ranges, with replies, @mentions, reactions, and attachments. (https://velt.dev/comments)
- **Co-editing**: CRDT merge across clients on the node tree. (https://velt.dev/multiplayer-editing)
- **Presence and cursors**: Live named cursors and selections in the editor. (https://velt.dev/presence)
- **Suggestions**: Propose changes as accept-or-reject suggestions, reviewed like a diff. (https://velt.dev/suggestions)
- **Notifications**: In-app, email, and Slack alerts on every comment and @mention. (https://velt.dev/notifications)
- **Recording**: Pin a quick voice, screen, or video clip in context on the editor. (https://velt.dev/recording)
- **Version history**: Named checkpoints on the document, saved and restored by API. (https://velt.dev/multiplayer-editing)
- **Single editor mode**: Run Velt review on a single editor instance without multiplayer. (https://velt.dev/multiplayer-editing)

## Agents

a brand-and-compliance agent flags an off-message line or a missing disclosure on the node and suggests the rewrite as a first-class user; a human approves or rejects, and on approve the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record of who allowed what.

## Setup

```bash
npm install @veltdev/react + @veltdev/lexical-crdt-react
```

## FAQ

**Comments only, or co-editing too?** Both. Velt adds threaded comments and conflict-free co-editing on the same Lexical editor.

**Do comments survive Lexical node-tree updates?** Yes. Robust anchoring binds each thread to its node, so a comment rides updates and re-renders instead of detaching.

**Do custom and decorator nodes work?** Yes. Velt anchors to any node or range, including custom and decorator nodes.

**Can an agent post on a node, with a human approving?** Yes. An agent posts a suggestion on the node as a first-class user, and a human approves or rejects before it lands.

**Do I need a backend?** No. Velt runs without you standing up a websocket fleet or merge backend.

**How is Velt priced?** On usage, not seats or integrations: you pay for documents with review activity in a month, with a free tier for development and early production.

---

# Let agents read your Velt review data and propose changes (beta)
https://velt.dev/libraries/mcp

The Velt MCP server gives any MCP-capable agent the review context on a document, comments, threads, and decisions, and lets it add comments and propose changes in-thread. Agents read what humans decided and propose the next change; a human approves before anything lands.

## What you get

- Agents read review context over MCP.
- Agents add comments and propose changes in-thread, with human approval required (write scope in beta).
- Works with any MCP client.

## Setup

Enable the Velt MCP server; docs velt.dev/docs/mcp/mcp.

## FAQ

**What can an agent do over MCP?** Read the review context on a document, including comments, threads, and decisions, and add comments or proposed changes in-thread.

**Is it read-only or can it write?** Agents can read review context on all plans. Write scope, adding comments and proposing changes, is in beta.

**Does a human still approve?** Yes, always. Any change an agent proposes requires human approval before it lands.

**How is Velt priced?** On usage, not seats or integrations: you pay for documents with review activity in a month, with a free tier for development and early production.

Your users expect to comment and co-edit in Monaco, and your AI agents need that same buffer with a human approving before they touch user work. Every quarter spent on this is a quarter not spent on your own product.

## Built for Monaco

Velt is the review and collaboration layer built for Monaco: your users and your AI agents work the same buffer, with comment threads anchored to the line, and every agent suggestion is a change a human approves before it lands.

## Features

- **Co-editing**: Conflict-free co-editing on the model. (https://velt.dev/multiplayer-editing)
- **Presence and cursors**: Live named cursors and selections in the buffer. (https://velt.dev/presence)

- **Version history**: Named checkpoints on the file, saved and restored by API. (https://velt.dev/multiplayer-editing)
- **Audit trail**: Every review on the file, exportable. (https://velt.dev/audit-trail)
- **Single editor mode**: Run Velt review on a single editor instance without multiplayer. (https://velt.dev/multiplayer-editing)

## Agents

a code-review agent flags a bug or style issue on the exact line and proposes the fix as a suggestion; your user approves or rejects it like a pull request, and on approve the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record of who allowed what.

## Setup

```bash
npm install @veltdev/react + @veltdev/monaco-crdt-react
```

## FAQ

**Comments only, or co-editing too?** Both. Velt adds threaded comments and conflict-free co-editing on the same Monaco instance.

**Do comments hold in large files?** Yes. Robust anchoring binds each thread to its line, so comments hold as the buffer grows and lines shift above them.

**Does the diff editor work?** Yes. Velt anchors comments to lines and selections in both the standard and diff editor views.

**Can an agent leave a review comment on a generated function, for a human to approve?** Yes. An agent posts a suggestion on the exact line as a first-class user, and a human approves or rejects it like a pull request.

**Do I need a backend?** No. Velt runs without you standing up a websocket fleet or merge backend.

**How is Velt priced?** On usage, not seats or integrations: you pay for documents with review activity in a month, with a free tier for development and early production.

# Comments and annotations, built for Nivo
https://velt.dev/libraries/nivo

Add comments and shared annotations, plus live presence, to your Nivo charts, for your users and your AI agents. Threads stay pinned to the data point as the chart re-renders, and every agent annotation lands for your reviewer to approve, so reviewers discuss the spike on the spike.

## Build this into Nivo yourself, and you rebuild it on every release.

Your users expect to comment and co-edit in Nivo, and your AI agents need that same chart with a human approving before they touch user work. Comments that survive Nivo's re-renders are a multi-quarter build, and the moment anchoring breaks, feedback lands on the wrong data point. Co-editing is the harder half: rolled by hand it means overwrites, lost work, and merge conflicts, the "my changes disappeared" bug reports, plus a websocket fleet and offline merge to keep alive. And the harder question is your agents: a useful agent needs to change the work, but an agent with write access to user content is what your buyers' security review blocks, so without a consent step you choose between an agent that is useful and an agent that is safe. Every quarter spent on this is a quarter not spent on your own product.

## Built for Nivo

Velt is the review and collaboration layer built for Nivo: your users and your AI agents work the same chart, with comment threads anchored to the data point and series, and every agent annotation is a change a human approves before it lands.

## Features

- **Agents as first-class users**: An analysis agent annotates the anomaly on the data point and proposes the caption as a first-class user; your reviewer approves it before it goes into the report, with a permanent record of who allowed what. (https://velt.dev/review-agents)
- **Comments**: Threaded comments on data points and series, with replies, @mentions, reactions, and attachments, that stay pinned to the point as the chart re-renders. (https://velt.dev/comments)
- **Annotations**: Shared, live-synced markup on the data point, anchored through re-renders, so every reviewer sees the same callouts on the same spike. (https://velt.dev/comments)
- **Presence and cursors**: Live named cursors and who is here right now, on the chart. (https://velt.dev/presence)
- **Notifications**: In-app, email, and Slack alerts on every comment and @mention, so a review never stalls. (https://velt.dev/notifications)

## Agents

An analysis agent annotates the anomaly on the data point and proposes the caption as a first-class user; your reviewer approves it before it goes into the report, with a permanent record of who allowed what.

## Setup

```bash
npm install @veltdev/react + @veltdev/nivo-react
```

## FAQ

**Comments and annotations, or co-editing?** Annotations on a rendered chart. A chart is a read surface, so the shared state is markup; comments and shared annotations both work.

**Do comments anchor to the data layer?** Yes. Threads stay pinned to the data point and series as the chart re-renders.

**Do they survive a re-render?** Yes. Anchoring is stable across data updates and chart re-renders.

**Can an agent annotate a point, for a human to approve?** Yes. An analysis agent posts an annotation on the data point as a first-class user; your reviewer approves it before it appears in the report, with a permanent record of who allowed what.

**Do I need a backend?** No. Velt runs the collaboration layer for you.

**How is Velt priced?** On usage, not seats or integrations: you pay for documents with review activity in a month, with a free tier for development and early production.

# Comments and co-editing, built for React Flow
https://velt.dev/libraries/react-flow

Add comments and co-editing, plus live presence, to your React Flow canvas, for your users and your AI agents. Threads stay pinned to the node as the graph moves, and every agent edit lands as a suggestion your users approve, so every comment stays on the node it was about.

## Build this into React Flow yourself, and you rebuild it on every release.

Your users expect to comment and co-edit in React Flow, and your AI agents need that same canvas with a human approving before they touch user work. Comments that survive as the React Flow graph moves are a multi-quarter build, and the moment anchoring breaks, feedback lands on the wrong node. - **Comments**: Threaded comments on nodes and edges, with replies, @mentions, reactions, and attachments, that stay pinned to the node as the graph moves. (https://velt.dev/comments)

An agent proposes a node or layout change on the canvas as a suggestion, as a first-class user; your user approves or rejects, and on approve the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record of who allowed what.

## Setup

```bash
npm install @veltdev/react + @veltdev/reactflow-crdt
```

## FAQ

**Comments only, or co-editing too?** Both. Comments anchor to nodes and edges; co-editing keeps the graph in sync across clients with CRDT conflict-free merge.

**Do custom nodes work?** Yes. Comments and presence attach to any node type, including custom nodes.

**Can two people co-edit the graph?** Yes. The CRDT adapter merges concurrent node moves, edge changes, and additions without overwrites.

**Can an agent propose a change, for a human to approve?** Yes. An agent posts a node or layout suggestion as a first-class user; your user approves or rejects it, and on approve the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record.

# Comments and co-editing, built for Slate
https://velt.dev/libraries/slatejs

Add comments and co-editing, plus live presence, to your Slate editor, for your users and your AI agents. Threads stay pinned to the node tree as the document changes, and every agent edit lands as a suggestion your users approve, so a comment survives a normalization instead of detaching from the block it was about.

## Build this into Slate yourself, and you rebuild it on every release.

Your users expect to comment and co-edit in Slate, and your AI agents need that same editor with a human approving before they touch user work. Comments that survive Slate's normalizations are a multi-quarter build, and the moment anchoring breaks, feedback lands on the wrong node. Co-editing is the harder half: rolled by hand it means overwrites, lost work, and merge conflicts, the "my changes disappeared" bug reports, plus a websocket fleet and offline merge to keep alive. And the harder question is your agents: a useful agent needs to change the work, but an agent with write access to user content is what your buyers' security review blocks, so without a consent step you choose between an agent that is useful and an agent that is safe. Every quarter spent on this is a quarter not spent on your own product.

## Built for Slate

Velt is the review and collaboration layer built for Slate: your users and your AI agents work the same editor, with comment threads anchored to the node, and every agent suggestion is a change a human approves before it lands.

## Features

- **Agents as first-class users**: Your AI agent comments and suggests on the editor as a first-class user; a human approves or rejects, and on approve the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record. (https://velt.dev/review-agents)
- **Comments**: Threaded comments on nodes and ranges, with replies, @mentions, reactions, and attachments. (https://velt.dev/comments)
- **Co-editing**: CRDT merge on the Slate document. (https://velt.dev/multiplayer-editing)
- **Presence and cursors**: Live named cursors and selections in the editor. (https://velt.dev/presence)
- **Suggestions**: Propose changes as accept-or-reject suggestions, reviewed like a diff. (https://velt.dev/suggestions)
- **Notifications**: In-app, email, and Slack alerts on every comment and @mention. (https://velt.dev/notifications)
- **Recording**: Pin a quick voice, screen, or video clip in context on the editor. (https://velt.dev/recording)
- **Version history**: Named checkpoints on the document, saved and restored by API. (https://velt.dev/multiplayer-editing)
- **Single editor mode**: Run Velt review on a single editor instance without multiplayer. (https://velt.dev/multiplayer-editing)

## Agents

a brand-and-compliance agent flags an off-message line on the node and suggests the rewrite as a first-class user; a human approves or rejects, and on approve the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record of who allowed what.

## Setup

```bash
npm install @veltdev/react + @veltdev/slate-crdt-react
```

## FAQ

**Comments only, or co-editing too?** Both. Velt adds threaded comments and conflict-free co-editing on the same Slate editor.

**Do comments hold across Slate normalizations?** Yes. Robust anchoring binds each thread to its node, so a comment survives normalizations instead of detaching.

**Do custom elements and voids work?** Yes. Velt anchors to any node or range, including custom elements and void nodes.

**Can an agent suggest on a node, with a human approving?** Yes. An agent posts a suggestion on the node as a first-class user, and a human approves or rejects before it lands.

**Do I need a backend?** No. Velt runs without you standing up a websocket fleet or merge backend.

**How is Velt priced?** On usage, not seats or integrations: you pay for documents with review activity in a month, with a free tier for development and early production.

# Comments and co-editing, built for SpreadJS
https://velt.dev/libraries/spreadjs

Add comments and co-editing, plus live presence, to your SpreadJS workbook, for your users and your AI agents. Threads stay pinned to the cell as the sheet recalculates, and every agent edit lands as a suggestion your users approve, so the question on a cell stays on that cell.

## Build this into SpreadJS yourself, and you rebuild it on every release.

Your users expect to comment and co-edit in SpreadJS, and your AI agents need that same workbook with a human approving before they touch user work. Comments that survive SpreadJS's recalcs are a multi-quarter build, and the moment anchoring breaks, feedback lands on the wrong cell. Co-editing is the harder half: rolled by hand it means overwrites, lost work, and merge conflicts, the "my changes disappeared" bug reports, plus a websocket fleet and offline merge to keep alive. And the harder question is your agents: a useful agent needs to change the work, but an agent with write access to user content is what your buyers' security review blocks, so without a consent step you choose between an agent that is useful and an agent that is safe. Every quarter spent on this is a quarter not spent on your own product.

## Built for SpreadJS

Velt is the review and collaboration layer built for SpreadJS: your users and your AI agents work the same workbook, with comment threads anchored to the cell, and every agent suggestion is a change a human approves before it lands.

## Features

- **Agents as first-class users**: Your AI agent comments and suggests on the workbook as a first-class user; a human approves or rejects, and on approve the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record. (https://velt.dev/review-agents)
- **Comments**: Cell-level comments with replies and @mentions, pinned to the cell through recalcs and across multiple sheets. (https://velt.dev/comments)
- **Co-editing**: CRDT shared cell state so two users write to the same workbook without overwrites. (https://velt.dev/multiplayer-editing)
- **Presence and cursors**: Live named cursors and selections on the sheet, so everyone knows who is where. (https://velt.dev/presence)
- **Suggestions**: Propose cell changes as accept-or-reject suggestions, reviewed like a diff. (https://velt.dev/suggestions)
- **Notifications**: In-app, email, and Slack alerts on every comment and @mention, so a review never stalls. (https://velt.dev/notifications)
- **Version history**: Named checkpoints for the workbook, saved and restored by API. (https://velt.dev/multiplayer-editing)
- **Audit trail**: Every change to the number, every approval, exportable. (https://velt.dev/audit-trail)

## Agents

A checking agent flags the cell where a formula breaks or a number misses the model and comments on it as a first-class user; your reviewer approves the correction, and on approve the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record of who allowed what.

## Setup

```bash
npm install @veltdev/react + @veltdev/spreadjs-crdt-react
```

## FAQ

**Comments only, or co-editing too?** Both. You can ship comments alone or add co-editing via the CRDT adapter; they are independent capabilities.

**Do comments hold across formulas and multiple sheets?** Yes. Comment threads are anchored to the cell reference, not the rendered position, so they survive recalculations and cross-sheet moves.

**Do large workbooks work?** Yes. The adapter is designed for production workbook sizes; anchoring is by cell reference, not DOM position.

**Can an agent flag an outlier cell, for a human to approve?** Yes. An agent posts a comment or suggestion on the cell as a first-class user, and a human approves or rejects before any value changes.

**Is there a record of who approved each change?** Yes. Every approval fires a webhook event and is written to the audit trail, exportable for compliance.

**How is Velt priced?** On usage, not seats or integrations: you pay for documents with review activity in a month, with a free tier for development and early production.

## Build this into SuperDoc yourself, and you rebuild it on every release.

Your users expect to comment and co-edit in SuperDoc, and your AI agents need that same document with a human approving before they touch user work. Comments that survive SuperDoc's docx edits are a multi-quarter build, and the moment anchoring breaks, feedback lands on the wrong paragraph. Co-editing is the harder half: rolled by hand it means overwrites, lost work, and merge conflicts, the "my changes disappeared" bug reports, plus a websocket fleet and offline merge to keep alive. Every quarter spent on this is a quarter not spent on your own product.

## Built for SuperDoc

Velt is the review and collaboration layer built for SuperDoc: your users and your AI agents work the same document, with comment threads anchored to the paragraph, and every agent suggestion is a change a human approves before it lands.

## Features

- **Agents as first-class users**: Your AI agent comments and suggests on the document as a first-class user; a human approves or rejects, and on approve the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record. (https://velt.dev/review-agents)
- **Comments**: On paragraphs and ranges, with replies, @mentions, and attachments. (https://velt.dev/comments)
- **Co-editing**: CRDT merge on the docx content, so two people work the same document without overwrites. (https://velt.dev/multiplayer-editing)
- **Presence and cursors**: Live presence on the document. (https://velt.dev/presence)
- **Suggestions**: Propose redlines as accept-or-reject suggestions. (https://velt.dev/suggestions)

- **Recording**: Pin a quick voice, screen, or video clip in context on the document. (https://velt.dev/recording)
- **Version history**: Named checkpoints on the document, saved and restored by API. (https://velt.dev/multiplayer-editing)
- **Audit trail**: Every markup and approval on the matter, exportable. (https://velt.dev/audit-trail)

## Agents

A clause-review agent flags an off-standard term on the paragraph and suggests the redline as a first-class user; a human approves or rejects, and on approve the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record of who allowed what.

## Setup

```bash
npm install @veltdev/react + @veltdev/superdoc-crdt-react
```

## FAQ

**Comments only, or co-editing too?** Both. SuperDoc is a docx editor so Velt wires full CRDT co-editing alongside comment threads on the same document.

**Do comments hold with docx fidelity?** Yes. Threads anchor to paragraphs by stable identifier, not byte offset, so they survive reformatting, copy-paste, and round-trips through docx.

**Do tracked changes interop?** Yes. Velt suggestions map to the tracked-change model so suggestions your agents propose appear alongside native tracked changes.

**Can an agent suggest a redline, for a human to approve?** Yes. An agent posts the suggestion on the paragraph as a first-class user, and a human approves or rejects before the change lands.

**Do I need a backend?** No. Velt handles the realtime sync and persistence; you wrap your app in VeltProvider with your API key and mount the adapter.

**How is Velt priced?** On usage, not seats or integrations: you pay for documents with review activity in a month, with a free tier for development and early production.

## Agents

A checking agent flags the cell where a value misses the model and comments on the row as a first-class user; your reviewer approves the correction, and on approve the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record of who allowed what.

## Setup

```bash

```

## FAQ

**Comments only, or co-editing too?** Both. You can ship comments alone or add co-editing via the CRDT adapter; they are independent capabilities.

**Can an agent flag a cell, for a human to approve?** Yes. An agent posts a comment or suggestion on the cell as a first-class user, and a human approves or rejects before any value changes.

# Nivo Charts
https://velt.dev/libraries/nivo-charts

Add comments, notifications, and review workflows to Nivo charts in minutes

[Start Free](https://console.velt.dev/?ref=library-nivo-charts) · [View Docs](https://docs.velt.dev/async-collaboration/comments/setup/chart-comments-setup/nivo-charts)

## Built for Nivo Charts

Deeply embedded in Nivo and works reliably as chart data and layouts change

### Comments on data points

Leave comments on different types of charts

### Sticky Across Filters

Comments that stick across aggregation and filters

### Real-time Presence and Cursors

View other users on your document

### User Mentions

Enable rich conversations with replies, @mentions, and reactions

### Notification

See what changes have been made to a shared document with timestamps

### Offline Storage

Keep working when the connection drops. Data will sync when you reconnect

## Production-Ready in Minutes

Install the Velt Nivo Charts extension. Test. Ship.

```tsx
<ResponsiveLine
    data={data}
    layers={[
        'grid', 'markers', 'axes', 'areas', 'points',
        // Add this function with VeltNivoChartComments
        // component to allow Velt comments inside Chart
        (chartComputedData) => {
            return (
                <VeltNivoChartComments
                    id="NivoLineChartExample"
                    chartComputedData={chartComputedData}
                    dialogMetadataTemplate={['label', 'value', 'groupId']}
                />
            );
        },
    ]}
/>
```

[View Docs](https://docs.velt.dev/async-collaboration/comments/setup/chart-comments-setup/nivo-charts)

## FAQ

### Will comments update as data changes?

Yes. Velt anchors each comment to a data point, series, or range and re-attaches as the underlying dataset is updated, filtered, or re-aggregated.

### Does this work with animated charts?

Yes. The integration tracks chart-computed coordinates after each render, so comments stay attached through transitions, animations, and re-layouts.

### Can I add comments only?

Yes. The chart-comments package can be installed and used standalone, without enabling presence, cursors, or notifications.

### Do I need backend infrastructure?

No. Velt provides a fully managed collaboration backend for comments, presence, and persistence — no server to run.

### How does pricing work?

Pricing is based on Monthly Active Collaborators who actively use Velt features, not raw connections or messages.

# Yjs
https://velt.dev/libraries/yjs

Run Yjs apps without building or operating realtime infrastructure

[Start Free](https://console.velt.dev/?ref=library-yjs) · [View Docs](https://docs.velt.dev/realtime-collaboration/crdt/setup/core)

## Built for YJS

Velt handles sync, persistence, and connections so Yjs apps stay reliable at scale

### Multiplayer Editing

Co-edit documents in real-time and see who is working with you

### Contextual Comments

Enable rich conversations with replies, @mentions, and reactions

### Real-time Cursors & Presence

Decide how users appear with fully customizable name tags and cursors

### User Mentions

Enable rich conversations with replies, @mentions, and reactions

### Notification

See what changes have been made to a shared document with timestamps

### Version History

See what changes have been made to a shared document with timestamps

### Single Editor Mode

Limit editing control to one user in collaborative scenarios

### Offline Storage

Keep working when the connection drops. Data will sync when you reconnect

## Production-Ready in Minutes

Install the Velt YJS extension. Test. Ship.

```tsx
import { useVeltCrdtStore } from '@veltdev/crdt-react';

function Component() {
  const { update } = useVeltCrdtStore<string>({ id: 'my-collab-note', type: 'text' });
  const onChange = (e) => update(e.target.value);
  return <input onChange={onChange} />;
}
```

[View Docs](https://docs.velt.dev/realtime-collaboration/crdt/setup/core)

## FAQ

### Is this required to use Yjs?

No, Yjs works independently, but Velt removes the need to run your own backend.

### Do I need to manage a Yjs server?

No, Velt provides a fully managed realtime server and persistence layer.

### Does this handle persistence automatically?

Yes, document state is persisted without custom database wiring.

### How does pricing work?

Pricing is based on real collaboration usage, not raw connections or messages.

### Can I still use Yjs directly?

Yes, Velt works alongside standard Yjs usage via a lightweight wrapper.

# Integrate Velt in AWS S3
https://velt.dev/integrations/aws-s3

*Category: Storage*

Integrate Velt collaboration features in AWS S3 with just 6 lines of code. Add comments, webhooks, and real-time features to your S3 applications quickly.

## Connect AWS S3

Go to advanced webhook configs and create a new endpoint for AWS S3

## Configure the payload

Take the event and model it for your consumption with simple javascript functions

## Unified API

Build smarter customer flows by connecting services through webhooks.

```ts
// Initialize the Velt CRDT extension
const { store, isLoading } = useVeltCodeMirrorCrdtExtension({ editorId });

useEffect(() => {
  if (!store || !editorRef.current) return;

  const startState = EditorState.create({
    doc: store.getYText()?.toString() ?? '',
    extensions: [
      basicSetup,
      yCollab(store.getYText()!, store.getAwareness(), { undoManager: store.getUndoManager() }),
    ],
  });

  viewRef.current = new EditorView({
      state: startState,
      parent: editorRef.current,
  });

  return () => viewRef.current?.destroy();
}, [store]);
```

[Live demo](https://console.velt.dev/) · [Docs](https://docs.velt.dev/)

# AI-native SaaS
https://velt.dev/for/ai-native-saas

Products where AI generates the work need the loop that makes the work shippable: agents propose through comments and suggestions, humans approve, memory keeps decisions consistent, and the audit trail proves oversight.

## Your AI can generate the work. Getting it approved is the hard part.

- Users turned off the AI the first time it changed something it shouldn't, and the feature you shipped became the feature they distrust.
- Your enterprise buyer's security review stalled on the AI feature, and the deal stalled with it.
- Agents need write access to be useful, and security says no, so the agent stays a demo instead of shipping into the product.

If your product generates drafts, suggestions, or changes your users must answer for, this page is for you.

## Agents propose. Humans approve.

Your users want agents that act. Nobody wants agents that act alone. Velt is the layer between an agent's suggestion and a change to your users' data. Every agent suggestion becomes a comment with an action attached. A human approves or rejects. On approval, the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record of who allowed what; on rejection, nothing happens and the rejection is logged. The agent never holds write access to your data.

### Agent proposes

The product's own agent posts a comment on the draft it generated: a rationale, the proposed action, and the payload your webhook will apply. The avatar is AI-labeled, so everyone in the document knows an agent is acting. The agent calls the same commenting API a human user would.

### Human decides

The owner reviews the proposal, and a teammate thread shows the deliberation: “@Priya ok to apply this to all 14 accounts?” High-stakes proposals route into a staged approval chain instead of a single click, so the consent step matches the stakes of the change.

### Webhook applies

On approve, the POST payload hits the customer's endpoint and the user's data changes only now. The agent proposed the change; the human allowed it; your service applied it. Nothing reached the user's data that a human did not accept.

### Audit records

An immutable line records who proposed, who allowed, what changed, and when. The trail is the evidence your security questionnaire asks for, written synchronously with the change rather than reconstructed after the fact.

## What AI-native teams buy first.

Each card links its feature page. Preview the UI, or read the code that renders it.

### Comments

Your agent's findings and proposals land as comments on the generated draft, anchored to the exact claim or cell, with Approve and Reject attached. An agent is just a user with type agent.

```
<VeltComments />
```

### Suggestions

Model-produced changes render as inline diffs on user content. Accept applies the change or fires your webhook; Reject leaves the data untouched.

```
<VeltSuggestions />
```

### Approval flows

High-stakes agent output routes through staged sign-off: order, quorum, conditions, rejection paths, and a record for every run.

```
<VeltApprovalFlow
  stages={["owner", "quorum", "confirm"]}
/>
```

### Audit trail

Every proposal, decision, and applied change, attributed and exportable. The page of the security questionnaire your AI feature currently fails.

```
POST /v2/activities/get
{ "data": { "documentId": "renewal-email" } }
```

### Memory

Your users' past decisions surface as precedent, so review of generated work stays consistent as output volume grows.

```
velt.memory.search({
  query: "prior renewal decisions",
});
```

### Presence

See your agents work: avatars show the agent in the document, cursors and selection show exactly what it is touching, follow mode rides along.

```
<VeltPresence />
```

## Agents propose. Your users decide.

For AI-native products, the stake is the user's data itself: the rows, fields, and content one unsupervised write can corrupt, and the trust that never comes back after it does. So every agent action in Velt arrives as a proposal: the generated draft, the model-produced change, the agent's output, each one a comment or suggestion with Approve and Reject attached. On approval, the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record of who allowed what; on rejection, nothing happens and the rejection is logged. The agent never holds write access to your data. This shape is reversible, so you can build opinionated flows on top later; uniform, so you ship one consent pattern everywhere instead of per-feature approval UIs; and audit-complete by construction. For higher-stakes actions, escalate the consent: from one click, to quorum, to type-the-name confirmation. When Velt's built-in review agents reach GA, they slot into this same loop as a first pass on generated drafts before your users ever look.

## AI-native products, in production.

Customers in this space include products where AI generates the work and the propose-approve-apply loop runs inside the product: agents post proposals as comments and suggestions, humans approve or reject, and approved changes fire through the customer's own webhook with an audit record their security review asks for.

## Consent before action, evidence after it.

Agent changes apply only through your webhook after human approval, and the audit trail records who allowed what.

### Human oversight by construction

Approval before action is the mechanism; immutable records are the evidence. For buyers that the EU AI Act actually covers, Article 14's human-oversight requirement maps directly to this loop, scoped to the features in scope and never implying every AI feature is.

### Data on your infrastructure

Content and user PII can stay on your infrastructure via per-feature data providers; Velt stores minimal identifiers.

### SOC 2 Type II, audit export

SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA support, and EU data residency options, with the exportable record of every proposal and decision that vendor security reviews ask for.

## FAQ

### Can agents change data in my product without approval?

Not through Velt. Agent suggestions arrive as comments. A human approves or rejects; on approve, the change fires through your webhook with a permanent record of who allowed what. Agents never need write access to your data.

### How is this different from the approval flow in the OpenAI Agents SDK?

The OpenAI SDK pauses your own agent's tool calls so a developer-defined approver can resume them. Velt is the review surface your end users see inside your product: comment threads, multi-step approval workflows, audit records, and notifications, working across humans and agents with any model or framework.

### Does Velt care which model or agent framework we use?

No. Your agent is a Velt user with type agent and talks to the same REST APIs humans use: it posts comments and suggestions with a rationale and a payload, and your webhook applies approved changes. Any orchestration that can call an API works.

### Do my users have to approve every single agent action?

No. You decide where the consent step sits: generated drafts can flow freely, and the approval gate guards changes to user data. For higher-stakes actions, escalate the consent: from one click, to quorum, to type-the-name confirmation (quorum routing via approval flows, beta).

### Can my users watch what an agent is doing?

Yes. Agents appear in presence like any user, so your users always know when an agent is in the document. Cursors and live selection show exactly what it is touching, and follow mode lets a user ride along while it works.

### We generate thousands of drafts a month. How does pricing work?

Velt is priced on usage, not seats: you pay for documents with review activity in a month (monthly active documents), and agents are users, not billed seats. There is a free tier for development and early production.

# Compliance
https://velt.dev/for/compliance

In policy management, regulatory filing, and risk and attestation platforms, review is the regulated control itself. Velt embeds that control in your product: staged sign-off with quorum, immutable audit records that export for examiners, and review agents for the mechanical checks.

## When the examiner asks, the answer is archaeology.

- A filing went out with a stale disclaimer because the check lived in a reviewer's head, not in the product.
- The examiner asked who approved a disclosure, and the answer was a reconstruction from email threads and meeting notes.
- Your buyer's procurement asked whether you support staged sign-off with quorum, and the honest answer was a roadmap slide.
- The same disclaimer language got re-litigated three quarters in a row because the reviewers who settled it left.

If your product carries policies, filings, or attestations that a named person is accountable for approving, this page is for you.

## One filing, from first draft to examiner export.

Velt runs one quarterly disclosure filing through the full review loop inside your product: an agent first pass on the mechanical checks, comment threads that resolve on the filing itself, staged quorum sign-off, an immutable record, and an examiner export. Both humans and agents act through the same primitives; nothing advances until a named person signs it.

### The filing lands

A quarterly disclosure filing is drafted in your product, with the controls it attests to linked on the record so the review and the thing being reviewed live in one place.

### Agent first pass

A review agent checks disclaimers, PII, and policy references and leaves each finding as a comment pinned to the exact line: “Required risk disclaimer missing for this product class.” Approve and Reject are attached; the finding is a proposal, and a human decides.

### Comments resolve on the artifact

The compliance officer answers the flagged disclosure line in a thread on the filing itself, with internal deliberation scoped to the team. A workflow step can require all comments to be resolved before the filing advances, and Memory keeps what was settled from being re-flagged.

### Staged quorum sign-off

The workflow routes the filing: the analyst submits, the compliance officer approves, then a quorum group where two of three officers must sign. Approve advances it, reject routes it back, and every transition is timestamped and attributed.

### The immutable record

Each finding, reply, and sign-off is captured automatically as it happens; immutability is on by default for new accounts, so the evidence stands even when the content it describes changes.

### Examiner export

The full chain pulls through the Get Activity Logs REST API as structured JSON, filtered by document, user, or time range, so the answer the examiner asks for is already assembled.

## What compliance platforms buy first.

Each card links its feature page. Preview the UI, or read the code that renders it.

### Audit trail

Who approved the filing, who signed the attestation, what the disclosure said when they signed: queryable by document, user, or time range, and exportable when the examiner asks.

```

```

### Approval flows

Staged sign-off with quorum: two of three compliance officers must approve before the filing advances, and reject routes it back with every prior attempt on the record.

```

  stages={["analyst", "officer", "quorum"]}
/>
```

### Review agents

First-pass checks on disclaimers, PII, and policy references, landing as comments a compliance officer accepts or rejects. Mechanical checks before human judgment.

```
velt.addReviewAgent({
  instructions: "flag missing risk disclaimers",
});
```

### Comments

Threads pinned to the policy section, the disclosure line, the control. Deliberation scoped to the team; the resolution stays on the artifact.

```
<VeltComments />
```

### Memory

Settled disclaimer language stays settled: past decisions surface as precedent, and agents stop re-flagging what reviewers already cleared.

```
<VeltMemory />
```

## Agents check the filing. A human signs it.

An agent that checks every disclosure against the policy library is a tireless first-pass reviewer. An agent that edits the filing on its own is a regulatory finding waiting to happen. In Velt, every agent finding lands as a comment with Approve and Reject attached. On approve, the fix applies through your webhook with a permanent record of who allowed it; on reject, nothing changes and the rejection is logged. The agent never holds write access to policies, filings, or attestations. In compliance, the stakes are the control itself: if AI can change the artifact without a name attached, the review your product sells stops being evidence.

## Compliance platforms, in production.

In policy management, regulatory filing, and risk and attestation platforms, review is the product's regulated control. Velt embeds staged sign-off, immutable records, and an examiner export inside the product, so the evidence is captured as it happens instead of reconstructed from email threads after the examiner asks.

## The review is the evidence.

This buyer resells review as a control, so the strip leads with the evidence answer.

### The evidence answer

Every comment, approval, and rejection is captured automatically with who, what, and when; immutability is on by default for new accounts; and the record exports through the REST API. SOC 2 Type II.

### EU AI Act, scoped

Article 14 requires demonstrable human oversight for high-risk AI systems under Annex III (credit, insurance, hiring, critical infrastructure, and essential services among them), enforceable from August 2, 2026. For products in or selling into that scope, Velt provides the mechanism (approval before action) and the evidence (a record of who approved what). It never implies the Act covers all AI products.

### Residency for regulated data

Data residency options include the EU; self-host data providers keep comment and review content plus user PII on your infrastructure, and Velt stores minimal identifiers.

## FAQ

### Our product is the system of record for regulated filings. Can Velt's records serve as examiner evidence?

The review layer is captured automatically: every comment, approval, and rejection with who, what, and when, queryable by document, user, or time range, and retrievable as structured JSON through the REST API. Immutability is on by default for new accounts, so records stand even when the content they describe changes.

### Can we require two of three compliance officers to sign before a filing advances?

Yes. Workflows support sequential and parallel steps, quorum rules (two of three must approve), conditional branching, and comment-gated steps that hold the filing until every thread resolves. Every transition is timestamped and attributed.

### Can AI run the disclaimer and PII checks without ever touching the filing?

Yes. A review agent's findings land as comments pinned to the exact line, each with Approve and Reject. On approve, the fix applies through your webhook with a record of who allowed it; on reject, nothing changes. The agent never holds write access to the filing.

### Our customers face EU AI Act obligations. Does this give them Article 14 evidence?

Article 14 applies to high-risk AI systems defined in Annex III (credit, insurance, hiring, critical infrastructure, and essential services among them), enforceable from August 2, 2026; it is not a universal obligation on every AI feature. If your product or your customers operate in that scope, Velt provides the mechanism (approval before action) and the evidence (a record of who approved what, when, and why). Talk to your counsel about whether you are in scope; see /governance.

### Our buyers are banks and insurers. Can review data stay on our infrastructure?

Cloud by default, with a hybrid model: self-host data providers keep comment and review content plus user PII on your infrastructure while Velt stores only minimal identifiers, with data residency options including EU. Velt is SOC 2 Type II audited and supports HIPAA workloads. See /self-hosting and /governance.

### How does pricing work when one filing is touched by a dozen reviewers?

Velt is priced on usage, not seats: you pay for documents with review activity in a month, so a filing reviewed by twelve people costs the same as one reviewed by two. There is a free tier for development and early production.

# Legal
https://velt.dev/for/legal

Contract platforms, CLM, and legal ops tools live on redlines and sign-off. Velt embeds that loop in your product: clause-anchored comments, suggestion-mode redlining accepted or rejected like a diff, and approval chains from counsel to partner to client, every change attributed.

## When redlines round-trip through Word.

- Redlines live in a Word file emailed back and forth, and your product is where the final version gets pasted.
- A comment about clause 7 pointed at clause 9 by the time counsel read it, because the contract moved underneath it.
- “Who changed the indemnification cap” took a weekend of version archaeology before the client call.
- Two associates marked up the same draft during a handoff and one set of redlines disappeared.

If your product carries contracts, NDAs, or matters that more than one lawyer marks up before a client signs, this page is for you.

## One contract, from first redline to attributed clause history.

Velt runs one counterparty contract through the full review loop inside your product: clause-anchored threads, suggestion-mode redlines accepted or rejected like a diff, an approval chain from counsel to partner to client, and an attributed history of every clause. Both humans and agents act through the same primitives; nothing changes the contract without a human accepting it.

### The contract lands

Counterparty paper, an NDA, is uploaded into your product, and the deal team opens review on the matter.

### Clause comments

Threads anchor to the clause, not the page: the indemnification cap gets a thread, the term clause gets another. Deal strategy stays in threads scoped to the internal team; the client never sees the negotiating-position debate.

### Redlines as suggestions

Counsel proposes replacement language on clause 7 inline; an agent proposes a fallback definition on the liability clause with its rationale attached. Each pending redline shows current and proposed language; the reviewer accepts or rejects like a diff, with a reason on reject. Your code applies accepted language; the SDK never mutates the contract.

### Counsel to partner to client

The workflow routes the contract in order: counsel approves the redlines, the partner approves the position, and the client's approver records the final decision as a user your product provisioned with access to this contract. Approve advances it, reject routes it back with the redlines attached, and every transition is timestamped and attributed.

### Attributed clause history

Who proposed the language, who accepted the redline, who approved the version, when, and the note they left: queryable by document, user, or time range. The history of clause 7 reads as one chain, not a stack of file versions.

## Agents propose the clause. Counsel accepts it.

## FAQ

### Can redlining happen inside our product instead of round-tripping Word files?

Yes. Proposed language lands inline on the exact clause as a pending suggestion showing current and proposed text; the reviewer accepts or rejects each one like a diff, with a reason on reject. Accept fires an event and your code applies the language, so nothing changes the contract without a name attached. Works in supported editors and your own custom components. Suggestions is in beta.

### Do comments stay pinned to the right clause as the contract changes?

Yes. Threads anchor to the content itself, with robust anchoring to text and complex elements, so the comment on clause 7 stays on clause 7 as the draft moves. If a suggestion's target disappears before review, it goes stale instead of applying.

### Can an approval chain run counsel to partner to client?

Yes, when the client's approver is a user in your product. The workflow routes steps in order, counsel to partner to the client's signer, with quorum available where two partners must approve; every decision is timestamped and attributed. Internal-only threads never reach the client. Approval flows is in beta.

### Can the client ever see our internal comments?

No, not when threads are scoped. Any thread can be limited to the author, the team, or specific people, and notifications generate only for what a user can access. The client sees the shared thread move; the deal team's deliberation never reaches their inbox.

### Partners review from phones between meetings. Does this work on mobile?

Yes. Velt is optimized for mobile web, works inside WebViews in native apps, and pure native apps can integrate through the REST APIs with your own native UI.

### How is this priced when matters spike and go quiet?

Velt is priced on usage, not seats: you pay for documents with review activity in a month, so a quiet matter costs nothing and a busy closing does not multiply per-user fees. There is a free tier for development and early production.

# Operations
https://velt.dev/for/operations

Operational decisions in supply chain, logistics, and field work need human sign-off with a record, often across organizations. Velt puts that sign-off inside your product: approval workflows on the record and its fields, comments scoped to your team or the counterparty, and notifications that reach reviewers in the yard, not just at a desk.

## When the approval never reaches the yard.

- A shipment sat at the dock for two days because the release approval sat unread in an inbox, with no way to escalate it inside your product.
- A counterparty read an internal note about their own rates, because your product has one comment stream for everyone instead of threads scoped to the team.
- The field crew never saw the inspection request, because they work from phones in a yard, not from a desk inside your web app.
- A customer audit asked who approved the substitution on the manifest, and the answer lived in a text thread on someone's phone.

If your product moves orders, shipments, or work orders that someone in another organization has to sign, this page is for you.

## One change order, two organizations, no phone tree.

Velt runs one change order from filed to signed inside your product: a review agent first pass on the rate, comment threads scoped to each side, a staged approval chain that crosses the org line, notifications that reach the field, and an audit record of every decision. Both humans and agents act through the same primitives; nothing changes without a human accepting it.

### The change order lands

The carrier cannot meet the delivery window, so the counterparty files a change order against the shipment record inside your product. The thread anchors to the record itself, not to an email about it.

### Agent first pass

A review agent checks the change order against the contract terms and leaves a comment pinned to the rate line: the revised rate is 9% over the contracted lane rate, flagged for commercial review. Approve and Reject are attached; the finding is advisory, and a human decides.

### Scoped comments

Two threads live on the same record. The internal thread, badged internal, debates absorbing the cost versus disputing the rate, and the counterparty cannot see it. The shared thread asks the counterparty to confirm the new delivery date, and they reply in your product instead of in an email chain about it.

### The approval chain across two orgs

The workflow routes the record: the ops lead approves, commercial approves the rate exception, then the counterparty's signer records the final decision. Both sides are users your product provisioned with access to this record, and every transition is timestamped and attributed.

### Notifications reach the field

The site supervisor gets the request by email, opens the record on mobile web, and approves from the yard. The counterparty's signer is notified of the shared thread and their step only, because notifications generate solely for what each user can access.

### The audit record

The full chain sits in one place: who was asked, who decided, and what changed on the record, queryable by document, user, or time range, and exportable when the customer audit comes.

## What operations platforms buy first.

Each card links its feature page. Preview the UI, or read the code that renders it.

### Approval flows

Release chains, rate exceptions, and change order sign-off: your customer's steps first, the counterparty's signer last. Approve advances the record; reject routes it back with every prior attempt attached.

```
<VeltApprovalFlow
  stages={["ops", "commercial", "counterparty"]}
/>
```

### Comments

Threads on the order, the manifest, and the field record. Internal deliberation stays scoped to the team; the counterparty reads only the thread meant for them.

```
<VeltComments />
```

### Notifications

The sign-off request leaves the building: in-app for dispatch, email for the yard, access-filtered so each organization sees only its own activity.

```
<VeltNotificationsTool />
```

### Audit trail

Who released the hold, who approved the substitution, and what changed on the manifest, queryable by record, user, or time range, and exportable when the customer audit lands.

```

{ "data": { "documentId": "ship-4127" } }
```

### Presence

See who is in the work order right now, your dispatcher or theirs, before two people release the same hold.

```
<VeltPresence />
```

## Agents flag the manifest. A human releases the truck.

An agent that reconciles a manifest against the order is a tireless first-pass reviewer. An agent that corrects the manifest on its own is a liability with a loading dock. In Velt, every agent finding lands as a comment with Approve and Reject attached. On approve, the correction applies through your webhook with a permanent record of who allowed it; on reject, nothing moves and the rejection is logged. The agent never holds write access to orders, inventory, or the counterparty's data. The stakes in operations are physical: a bad automated write is not a rollback, it is a truck at the wrong dock, a crew on the wrong site, a counterparty reading a number they were never meant to see.

## Operations teams, in production.

Operations platforms run sign-off on orders, shipments, work orders, and change orders across organizations, where the reviewer is often in a yard, a truck, or a job site rather than at a desk. They embed approval chains, visibility-scoped comments, and the audit export their customers' auditors ask for, instead of routing release decisions through phone trees and forwarded email.

## Built for the org line and the customer audit.

In operations the leading concern is what crosses between organizations, so the strip leads with residency and counterparty visibility.

### Counterparty visibility is a security feature

Per-thread visibility scopes and access-filtered notifications decide what crosses the org line. Internal activity stays internal, and notifications generate only for the documents and threads a user can access.

### Residency for global supply chains

Data residency options including the EU. Self-host data providers keep order, shipment, and comment content plus user PII on your infrastructure, while Velt stores minimal identifiers.

### The audit answer

SOC 2 Type II, with immutable review records and export for customer audits.

## FAQ

### Can an approval run across two companies, our customer's team and their counterparty?

Yes, when both sides are users in your product. Your product provisions the counterparty's reviewers as users with access to the shared record; the workflow routes steps to either side's people in order, and every decision is timestamped and attributed. Internal-only threads and notifications never reach them.

### Can we keep internal comments invisible to the counterparty?

Yes. Any thread can be scoped to the author, the team, or specific people, and notifications generate only for documents and threads a user can access. The counterparty sees their shared thread move; your customer's internal deliberation never reaches their inbox.

### Our reviewers are in yards, trucks, and job sites, not at desks. How do they approve anything?

Velt is optimized for mobile web, works inside WebViews in native apps, and pure native apps can integrate through the REST APIs with your own native UI. The request also travels out of the product: email through your SendGrid account or any service via webhooks, and your own channels via webhooks.

### We review orders and work orders, not documents. Does the model fit?

Yes. A document in Velt is any unit of work your product renders: an order, a shipment record, a work order, an inspection. Comments anchor to records and fields, approvals attach to the record, and the audit trail follows it.

### What do we show the customer's auditors when they ask who released a hold?

The record. Every comment, approval, and rejection is captured automatically with who, what, and when, queryable by document, user, or time range, and exportable. The answer to "who approved the substitution" is a query, not an archaeology project.

### How does pricing work when thousands of counterparty users touch a record once a month?

Velt is priced on usage, not seats: you pay for documents with review activity in a month, so occasional counterparty reviewers do not multiply your bill. There is a free tier for development and early production.

# Sales enablement
https://velt.dev/for/sales-enablement

Content platforms live and die on review cycles: brand, legal, and client approval on every asset. Velt puts that loop inside your platform: comments on decks and emails, approval chains with quorum, AI first-pass brand and compliance checks, and an audit trail for regulated clients.

## Where campaign reviews actually stall.

- Client feedback on the deck arrives as annotated screenshots and reply-all email, because threads, mentions, and anchoring in your own platform is a two-quarter build that keeps slipping.
- An enterprise prospect asks whether their legal team can sign off on every email before it sends, and the honest answer is a workflow engine you would have to build to close the deal.
- A bank or pharma client asks who approved last quarter's campaign, and the proof is a forwarded email, a screenshot, and a Slack thread someone deleted.
- Your AI already drafts emails and checks brand guidelines, but enterprise buyers will not turn it on while nothing sits between the AI and the client's content.

Every one of these is the review loop living outside your product. Below is what it looks like inside.

## One campaign email, draft to client-approved.

Velt runs a campaign email through the full review loop inside your platform: comment threads on the draft, an AI first pass against the client's brand guidelines, a staged approval chain that ends with the client, and an audit record of every decision. Both humans and agents act through the same primitives; nothing changes without a human accepting it.

### The draft

A marketer finishes a promo email for a bank client in your email builder and @mentions the brand lead on the subject line: “Too close to the competitor's tagline?” The thread anchors to the subject line itself, not to a screenshot of it.

### Agent first pass

A review agent checks the draft against the client's brand guidelines and disclosure rules and leaves three findings as comments anchored to the exact elements: the CTA button is off the client's palette, the APR claim is missing its required disclaimer, the footer carries an outdated logo. Each finding has a suggested fix with Approve and Reject.

### The consent step

The marketer accepts the disclaimer fix and the text change applies as a suggestion; she rejects the logo finding because the client signed off on that version last week. Nothing reached the email that a human did not accept. With Memory, the agent reads that rejection and stops re-flagging the logo.

### The approval chain (beta)

The email enters the chain the agency defined in your UI on Velt's approval APIs: brand review, then legal, then the client's approver. Each reviewer is notified in-app, by email, or in Slack, and the chain does not advance while comments on the draft stay unresolved.

### The record

The client clicks Approve and the email is cleared to send, with a timestamped record of who was asked, who approved, what the agent flagged, and what changed. The next audit question is answered before it is asked.

## FAQ

### Can our clients approve a deck or an email without logging into a separate tool?

Client approvers act inside your product: the approval request reaches them by email or Slack with a link to the asset, and approve or reject happens on the asset itself, recorded.

### Can we keep internal comments hidden from the client?

Yes. Comment visibility is scoped per thread: only me, my team, or specific people. Internal debate about the client's brand feedback stays invisible to the client reviewing the same asset.

### Can an AI check every email against a client's brand guidelines before a human looks?

Yes. Review agents take plain English instructions, for example “flag off-brand colors, missing disclaimers, and outdated logos,” and leave findings as comments with suggested fixes a human accepts or rejects.

### What do we show a bank or pharma client who audits campaign approvals?

An exportable record per asset: who was asked, who approved, what the AI flagged, what changed, and when. Records are queryable by document, user, workflow, or time range.

### Our emails and landing pages are built in a custom drag-and-drop builder. Does this work there?

Yes. Comments, suggestions, and approvals anchor to elements, not to editors, so they work in custom builders and canvases, with prebuilt setups for Tiptap, CodeMirror, and 10 other editor libraries.

### How does pricing work for a platform with thousands of campaign assets?

Usage-based on monthly active documents: you pay for the decks, emails, and pages that had review activity in a month, not per seat and not per asset stored. There is a free tier for development and early production.
